programme.title: Registry Modules and Version Constraints Follow Along
programme.topic: Terraform Registry Modules and Version Constraints
programme.outcome: Find and use a public Terraform Registry module; pin and verify an exact module version; practice pessimistic, compound and exact module version constraints; use terraform init -upgrade to change the selected registry module release; prove that .terraform.lock.hcl does not lock remote module versions; create and repair one unsatisfiable module-version failure; run reviewed plan/apply/destroy workflows without creating cloud resources; and safely remove all local training artifacts. This intentionally adds practical registry module-version coverage not claimed by the local-module refactoring lab.
programme.region: Terraform public Registry global resources and local workstation only; no AWS or other cloud resources are created.
programme.statusNotice: **Status:** Offline authoring manuscript only — not locally validated, imported, accepted, approved, published or fingerprinted.

examObjectivesCovered.text: Initialize, validate, plan, apply and destroy during the registry-module workflow

completionDefinition: The learner finds cloudposse/label/null in the public Terraform Registry and verifies baseline version 0.24.1 and current lab target 0.25.0.
The root module calls the registry module with an exact version and uses module inputs and outputs without creating any cloud resource.
terraform init installs the exact module version and .terraform/modules/modules.json is used to verify the selected release.
A saved plan is reviewed before every apply in the lab.
The learner broadens the constraint to ~> 0.24 and deliberately upgrades to 0.25.0.
The learner narrows the constraint to ~> 0.24.0 and proves selection returns to 0.24.1.
The learner practices the compound range >= 0.24.0, < 0.25.0 and the exact pin = 0.25.0.
The learner proves .terraform.lock.hcl does not lock remote module version selections.
An impossible >= 1.0.0 module constraint fails during init and is repaired by restoring the exact 0.25.0 pin.
The learner can distinguish public registry module version management from local-module creation/refactoring.
A saved destroy plan confirms no managed infrastructure exists, then all lab-only plan, cache, state and configuration files are removed in reverse-dependency order.

phases.title: Prepare and discover registry modules
phases.goal: Verify Terraform, understand the exam gap this lab fills, and inspect a real versioned public registry module before writing configuration.

phases.title: Install and use an exact module version
phases.goal: Call a public registry module at an exact version, initialize it, inspect the downloaded module metadata, and run the normal Terraform workflow safely.

phases.title: Broaden a constraint and upgrade the module
phases.goal: Change the module constraint, deliberately allow a newer compatible release, run init -upgrade, and prove which version Terraform selected.

tasks.title: Verify Terraform and the lab boundary
tasks.goal: Confirm Terraform is installed and understand that this lab creates no cloud infrastructure or credentials.
tasks.whyItMatters: The goal is module source and version behavior, so cloud authentication would add noise and risk without helping objective 5d.
tasks.examRelevance: Objectives 5a, 5c and especially 5d are the focus. This lab intentionally adds registry module version-management practice that a local-module refactoring lab does not claim.

browserSteps.instruction: Open Windows PowerShell. If you use Bash instead, the Bash commands are supplied where syntax differs.
Run terraform version. If Terraform is missing, install it from the official HashiCorp install page before continuing.
Do not sign in to AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, HCP Terraform, or any other cloud for this lab. No credentials are required.
Record the safety boundary: the public Terraform Registry is used only to download module source code; the selected training module defines zero managed resources.
Record the learning boundary: this programme does not teach creating or refactoring a local child module. It teaches registry source addresses and practical module version constraints.

browserSteps.instruction: Open https://registry.terraform.io in a browser.
Search for cloudposse/label/null and open the module page.
Confirm the module source address shown by the Registry is cloudposse/label/null.

Confirm version 0.25.0 is also available and is the current latest release used by this lab.
Open the Resources tab and confirm the module defines 0 resources. This is why the lab can safely run plan and apply without cloud credentials.
Open the Outputs tab and confirm the module exposes an id output.
Do not copy a latest-only example into the lab yet; the next task pins an exact baseline version so version changes are deliberate.

tasks.title: Initialize and inspect the exact downloaded module
tasks.goal: Run terraform init, then inspect the module cache metadata to prove Terraform installed version 0.24.1.
tasks.whyItMatters: Registry module versions are resolved during initialization; the downloaded module metadata gives direct evidence of the selected release.
tasks.examRelevance: Objective 5d is practical here: Terraform resolves an exact registry module version and installs it during init.

browserSteps.instruction: Open PowerShell or Bash in C:\terraform-labs\fa-registry-modules-terraform.
Run terraform init.
Read the init output and find the line that says it is downloading cloudposse/label/null 0.24.1 for training_label.
Open the .terraform folder that init created. This is local working data and must not be committed as source.
Open .terraform/modules/modules.json and find the training_label entry. Confirm its Version is 0.24.1.
If .terraform.lock.hcl exists, do not use it as proof of the module version. HashiCorp documents that the dependency lock file currently tracks provider selections, not remote module selections.
Do not manually edit files under .terraform/modules. Terraform owns the downloaded cache.

tasks.title: Broaden the version constraint with ~> 0.24
tasks.goal: Replace the exact module pin with ~> 0.24 and understand exactly which version range that syntax permits.
tasks.whyItMatters: The pessimistic operator is easy to misread; the number of version components changes the upper bound.
tasks.examRelevance: Objective 5d includes module version management. HashiCorp documents that ~> allows the right-most specified component to increment.

browserSteps.instruction: Open main.tf.
Replace only version = "= 0.24.1" with version = "~> 0.24".
Do not change the source address or any module inputs.
Understand the constraint before running init: ~> 0.24 allows 0.24 and later 0.x releases but not 1.0 or later. Therefore 0.25.0 is acceptable.
Save main.tf.

tasks.title: Run init -upgrade and prove Terraform selects 0.25.0
tasks.goal: Force Terraform to reconsider the already-installed module and select the newest version allowed by ~> 0.24.
tasks.whyItMatters: Re-running plain init does not necessarily replace an already-installed module; -upgrade is the deliberate signal to update module source selections.
tasks.examRelevance: Objective 5d is demonstrated by changing a registry module constraint and using init -upgrade to select a newer allowed release.

tasks.title: Prove module versions are not locked in .terraform.lock.hcl
tasks.goal: Compare module installation metadata with Terraform dependency lock behavior and explain where the selected remote module version is remembered.
tasks.whyItMatters: A common exam and real-world mistake is assuming .terraform.lock.hcl locks both providers and registry modules.
tasks.examRelevance: HashiCorp states that the dependency lock file currently tracks provider dependencies only; remote module versions are re-selected from their constraints.

browserSteps.instruction: Open .terraform/modules/modules.json and locate training_label Version 0.25.0.
Look in the root folder for .terraform.lock.hcl.
If no lock file exists, note that this configuration has no provider dependency requiring a lock selection.
If a lock file exists because of a local Terraform behavior or prior experiment, search it for cloudposse/label/null and confirm it does not contain a remote module version selection.
State the rule: module version constraints live in the module block; exact pins are the way to force the same registry module version across fresh installations.

cliBlocks.title: PowerShell - compare module metadata and lock file
Bash - compare module metadata and lock file
cliBlocks.content:
cat .terraform/modules/modules.json
test -f .terraform.lock.hcl && echo "lock file exists" || echo "no lock file"
if [ -f .terraform.lock.hcl ]; then grep -F "cloudposse/label/null" .terraform.lock.hcl || true; fi

expectedResults: modules.json shows the selected module version.
.terraform.lock.hcl is not used to pin the remote module version.
The learner can explain why an exact module version constraint provides reproducible registry module selection.

verificationChecks.text: The selected module version is visible in modules.json.
No cloudposse/label/null module selection is treated as a provider lock entry.
The learner can distinguish provider locking from remote module version constraints.

tasks.whyItMatters: Adding the patch component changes the pessimistic upper bound, which is a practical version-constraint distinction worth seeing directly.
tasks.examRelevance: Objective 5d: manage module versions with precise version ranges rather than assuming all ~> expressions behave the same.

tasks.title: Create an impossible module version constraint

tasks.title: Review Registry module and version-constraint exam points
tasks.goal: Turn the completed commands into a clear Terraform Associate 004 mental model for objectives 5a, 5c and 5d.
tasks.whyItMatters: The hands-on work matters only if you can explain the general Terraform behavior without relying on this one module.
tasks.examRelevance: Official exam mapping: 5a module sourcing, 5c using modules, and 5d managing module versions.

browserSteps.instruction: State the registry source rule: a public registry module source uses namespace/name/provider syntax, such as cloudposse/label/null.
State the version rule: the version argument is available for modules sourced from a registry; local filesystem modules do not use the version argument.
State the init rule: terraform init downloads child modules; terraform init -upgrade deliberately reconsiders already-installed module versions against the current constraints.
State the exact-pin rule: = 0.25.0 allows only 0.25.0.
State the pessimistic rule shown in the lab: ~> 0.24 allowed 0.25.0, while ~> 0.24.0 kept selection within the 0.24.x line.
State the compound rule: >= 0.24.0, < 0.25.0 expresses explicit lower and upper bounds.
State the lock-file rule: .terraform.lock.hcl currently records provider selections, not remote module version selections.
State the failure rule: if no module release satisfies the configured constraint, initialization fails before plan/apply.

State the boundary with the separate local-module refactoring lab: local module structure/refactoring and registry module release selection are different skills; this Follow Along intentionally covers the latter.
